Title and Team: Dux Carota Anti-Earth Gardening Association
Team Number: 5
Challenge Division: Middle School
Team members names: Leonardo Dinner, Ellie Chong, Elliot Phanthanusorn, Kayla Ong, Sam 
Barnhoorn
Rabbit Manure: a viable candidate for soil enhancement and legume success in
lunar regolith simulant
Background
The whirlwind advancement in technology since the 1969 lunar landing has brought humanity
closer to their dreams of colonies in space and on the moon. As missions increase in length, astronauts
look to minimize the amount of food and fuel they have to pack (Earth payload) in order to stay alive.
Plants, which can generate both oxygen and food, would be desirable during extended stays in these
extraterrestrial environments. After the Apollo 11 mission, NASA studied samples of collected moon
rock, known as lunar regolith, to determine if plants were able to use it in place of Earth soil. The lunar
regolith was analyzed and then used to plant a variety of plants. Unfortunately, plants showed severe
stress and stunted growth in this regolith, possibly due to a lack of nutrients, oxidative stress, and toxic
salts and metals. Since the supply of lunar regolith was limited, a lunar regolith simulant was developed
in order to conduct more research. [https://exolithsimulants.com/] Duri et al. discovered that organic
material such as compost and manure were able to encourage better plant growth. As the simulants did
not have many nutrients, they acted mainly as a mechanical anchorage for roots. The optimal ratio of
organic matter to simulant seemed to range between 1:1 to 3:1. The authors concluded organic matter
increased growth success by increasing water and/or nutrient availability to the plant. [Duri et al, 2022]
This study aims to explore the use of rabbit manure as both organic matter and nutrient source.
Rabbit manure comes in the form of dry pellets, which break down quickly, does not burn plants
because it does not contain as much ammonia as other manures, and has a reduced amount of
pathogens or antibiotics. Despite its high nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium percentages, rabbit
manure does not smell strongly, and is easy to handle. It can thus be used as packing material or even
replace foam cushions, reducing its payload impact on space missions. Previous studies revealed that
plants grown in lunar regolith had stunted root growth, and an upregulation of two genes associated
with phosphate starvation. Rabbit manure has one of the highest percentages of bioavailable
phosphorus, which roots need for optimal growth. Thus, rabbit manure has the potential to increase
successful plant growth in lunar regolith simulant.
Experimental Design:
While a ratio of 30:70 of regolith to organic matter was found to be the optimal conditions from
the manure study [Caporale et al, 2023], the constraints of Plant the Moon challenge indicated that 50%
of the material for planting must be lunar regolith in order to minimize any payload transported from
Earth. Exolith LHS1, a high-fidelity moon dirt simulant was used to mimic lunar regolith. Six pots with
450mL capacity per cup were filled with varying concentrations of lunar regolith, potting soil, and
rabbit manure. The first pot, a control, was composed of 50% simulant and 50% potting soil. The
second pot was also a control, and consisted of 50% potting soil and 50% rabbit manure. The third pot
had 50% simulant, 40% potting soil, and 10% rabbit manure. The fourth pot had 50% simulant, 30%
potting soil, and 20% rabbit manure. The fifth pot had 50% simulant, 10% potting soil, and 40% rabbit
manure. The sixth pot had 50% simulant and 50% rabbit manure. A second set of the same

concentrations was set up, giving 12 pots total. 5 seeds per pot were planted, in order to harvest at
different periods during the growth cycle to evaluate plant health and development. Purple bush beans
were chosen due to their ability to sprout, provide nourishment (all parts of the plant are edible and
beans provide protein as well as fiber and vitamins), and are hardy and do not need additional supports.
Table 1 below summarizes the growing conditions. See Figure 1 in Photos at the end of the report for a
picture of the set-up.
Table 1: Growing Conditions
The samples were initially watered once a week by gently soaking the entire sample in water
and removing excess water. As the plants grew larger and required more water, more frequent watering
was done for weeks 6, 7, and 8. On week 3, the plants were hardened outside in the sun for 2 hours in
the morning during the day. After this was done, the plants were placed in direct sunlight during the day
for weeks 4-8. Plants remained indoors at night.
Hypothesis
We think bush bean seeds grown in lunar regolith enriched with rabbit manure will grow more,
and have longer, more robust root systems. This is because rabbit manure acts as a fertilizer for both
nitrogen and phosphorus. Thus, rabbit manure will reverse the nitrogen/phosphorus starved conditions
of regolith soil by providing bioavailable nutrients for the plants.
Independent Variables/Dependent Variables:
The independent variable, or what is varied during this experiment is the amount of rabbit
manure. The dependent variable is the length of root and stem of the bean plant. The controlled
constant will be the lunar regolith simulant. 
Measurement and Procedures:
As the growing period was 8 weeks, root measurements were taken for weeks 1, 3, 5, 7 and 8. 
However, visual inspection could be done every week. When measurement was taken, the biomass 
(root+stem+leaves) was harvested by physically removing one plant from the container, placed next to 
a ruler and measured. Not all samples germinated and every effort was made to find the plant.

Unfortunately a few samples which did not germinate decomposed and not all biomass samples 
were able to be located. Weeks 1, 5, and 8 were photographed in order to record visual differences of 
the plants in different soil proportion environments.
The pH of the soil was measured for weeks 1 and 8. 
Controls:
In order to keep the amount of lunar regolith consistent, there were two controls. The first 
control of 0% rabbit manure (RM) had 1 cup lunar regolith and 1 cup potting soil with no amendments.
The second control had 1 cup rabbit manure and 1 cup potting soil. This second control is how the plant
would do on Earth, so in case there were any problems with the potting soil, rabbit manure, or growing 
containers used.
Results:
During the initial planting, the pH of the soil was measured to be 8.5 for all samples which 
contained lunar regolith. The water used to wet the soil had a pH of 7.5. Control 2 of potting soil and 
RM had a pH of 7.1. 
After 1 week of watering, germination (seed sprouting) was measured and presented in Table 2 
below. Some seeds had floated to the top despite being planted at a depth of 1 inch. The lunar regolith 
was not only hydrophobic, but also seemed to either push the seeds to the top or to sink them too far to 
be found. Control sample 2, 20% RM, and 50% RM samples all showed signs of germination 
(beginning of the lengthening of the hypocotyl, branching out of the first root). In the sample 
containing 40%, fungus had begun to grow.
Table 2: Week 1 Observations
In week 2, the first leaves could be seen in Control Sample 2, 40% RM, and 50% RM. Despite 
the fungus, the 40% RM had some growth. The fungal samples were isolated to prevent further 
spread. It was discovered that the 50% RM sample had twice the amount of expected bean plants, and 
was possibly double-planted during the initial planting stage. 
In week 3, some seeds in the 10% sample were seen to be decomposing, although no fungus 
grew in the sample. This observation was interesting because it was possible the lunar regolith was 
preventing fungus growth. Some activity was observed in the 20% and 40% sample, but already much 
slower than the control. Some root activity was observed in the 20% and 40% sample, but already 
much slower than the control. Some fungus was observed in the 50% RM sample, but the plants were 
growing vigorously and did not seem to be affected by the fungus.
In week 4, the fungus was present in the 40% and 50% RM samples. The plants in the 40% RM 
seemed much weaker and were on the verge of dying, but the 50% did not seem affected.

In week 5, an unfortunate mechanical injury happened to the 50% RM sample and is noted here,
as it did not grow as vigorously as expected for week 7. Control 2 had a normal expected growth 
pattern, with a more dense root ball, longer stem and larger leaves. There was no activity detected in 
the 10% and in fact all the seeds were missing. The 20% and 40% RM had noticeable but retarded 
growth.
In week 6, the plants in the 40% RM sample began to wilt. It was not able to be determined 
whether this was due to fungus or lunar regolith stress. The 20% RM sample could be visually seen to 
attempt to grow out of the soil and spread its first leaves. It was noted that perhaps the challenge of 
growing through the soil and not germination resulted in a lack of successful plants for the 10 and 20 
percent sample.
In week 7, possibly due to the rains and outdoor conditions, the fungus retreated and was almost
undetectable. However, the sample of 40% RM continued to do poorly. The plants in 20% RM were 
alive and attempting to bend out of the regolith mixture, but seemed to have difficulties. The 
specimens were curved in nature, and too weak to straighten out.
In week 8, the last observation period, the plants were lined up and photos were taken of the 
root length and plant length of all the samples. The control with just lunar regolith and potting soil, 
10%, and 20% failed to successfully grow. The 20% RM was able to stay alive, but the plant was 
warped in a circle and the leaves did not spread out. The control with potting soil and RM, 40% and 
50% RM were able to grow, although the 40% was affected by fungus and died by week 8. The 50% 
RM was able to grow but the leaves and roots were not as healthy or long as the control. However, 
they seemed to be robust enough to produce bean fruit, should the experiment have continued. The pH 
of the final plants were 8.0 for samples 1, 3 and 4, 7.4 for samples 4-5, and 7.1 for the control sample.

Conclusions: 
We found germination and plant growth was possible using lunar regolith simulant as long as 
20-50% of rabbit manure was used. The more RM, the better the growth and health of the plant, even 
at full rabbit manure (no potting soil). Just potting soil+lunar regolith simulant without RM was 
unsuccessful in sustaining plant growth. Our hypothesis that RM provided nutrients such as nitrogen

and phosphorous, not just organic matter to retain moisture is correct. Sterilization of the RM would be
a critical requirement, as the fungus present in RM appears to be deadly to new plants. However, if the 
plant survived after 5 weeks or was not exposed until then, there seemed to be a resistance to the 
fungus which would then be destroyed or minimized by solar radiation. It is of interest to note that no 
fungus grew in the samples that had a larger percentage of lunar regolith, suggesting its use as a 
fungicide. The bean plants used were able to survive in varying degrees, and could additionally be 
used as green fertilizer even if they did not provide food. This is important in the first stage of planting
on the moon, as the availability of nutrients and soil would be limited.
